patient.name: Chloe Adeyemi
patient.complaint: Vomiting, abdominal pain and drowsiness after 3 days of dysuria and fever
background: Type 1 diabetes since age 12 (insulin detemir twice daily, NovoRapid with meals)
Skipped insulin doses for 2 days because she was not eating
University student, lives in halls in Camden

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young person with type 1 diabetes (or a new presentation) who has vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria and deep rapid breathing, and a gas showing low pH and bicarbonate. They also test severity grading, diabetic ketosis vs DKA, and complications such as hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

points: **Brought to ED** by her flatmate, drowsy but rousable
**Passing large volumes of urine**, very thirsty
Abdomen soft, diffusely tender, **right loin tenderness**

visual.title: Where Chloe's pain is
visual.caption: DKA pain is **central and diffuse** (epigastric/periumbilical) with a soft abdomen. Chloe's extra **right flank** tenderness is her precipitant: pyelonephritis.

steps.text: DKA abdominal pain is real and can mimic a surgical abdomen, but it settles as the acidosis is corrected.

steps.q: Before any gas is back, which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Type 1 diabetes + missed insulin + infection + vomiting, polyuria, Kussmaul breathing and acetone breath = DKA until proven otherwise. The pyelonephritis is the **precipitant**, not the whole story.

steps.lead: Chloe has **type 1 diabetes** and has the two classic precipitants together: an **infection** (likely urinary) and **missed insulin doses**.
Her CBG of 28.4, polyuria, thirst, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness, **Kussmaul breathing**, tachycardia, hypotension and fruity breath tick almost every box on this list.

steps.title: Spotting DKA at the front door
nodes: Unwell patient with diabetes (or new thirst, polyuria, weight loss)
steps.caption: All three parts of the triad (glucose, ketones, acidosis) are needed. Ketones without acidosis is diabetic ketosis.

steps.title: Venous blood gas on arrival
steps.text: Urine dipstick: glucose 4+, **ketones 3+**, nitrites positive, leucocytes 2+.

visual.title: Chloe's venous pH against the DKA bands
visual.label: Chloe 7.14
visual.caption: pH 7.1–7.19 with bicarbonate <10 is **moderate**. Severe needs pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <5; mild is pH 7.2–7.29 with bicarbonate <15.

steps.q: Using pH and bicarbonate, how severe is Chloe's DKA?
steps.r: pH 7.14 sits in 7.1–7.19 and bicarbonate 8 is <10 but not <5, so this is **moderate** DKA. Severe would need pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <5.

steps.lead: Chloe's pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8, ketones 5.2 and urine ketones 3+ place her in the **moderate** band.
Chloe's potassium is **5.6 now**, but it will fall once insulin starts. She is 21, so cerebral oedema is less likely than in a child, but her GCS still needs watching.

visual.title: ECG if potassium falls during treatment
visual.caption: **Hypokalaemia**: small, flattened T waves and a **prolonged PR interval**. The opposite picture, tall tented T waves and a wide QRS, is hyperkalaemia.

steps.text: This is what Chloe's ECG would look like if her potassium were allowed to drop to about 2.8 mmol/L on insulin, the most common complication of DKA.
DKA abdominal pain and vomiting can mimic a **surgical abdomen** or gastroenteritis. 'Type 1 diabetes + vomiting + deep rapid breathing' = DKA. **Ketones negative** argues against it.

**Infection** is the most important precipitant. Every DKA stem hides one (UTI, pneumonia, gastroenteritis), or missed insulin, or a **new diagnosis** of type 1 diabetes (weight loss, thirst, polyuria in a teenager).

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (bedside capillary glucose and ketones) and 'Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?' (venous blood gas). They also ask for the gas pattern (raised anion gap metabolic acidosis), resolution criteria, and which parameter to monitor (potassium, mental status).

points: Triage bedside tests done within minutes

steps.lead: Chloe's bedside capillary ketones and glucose (BM) are done before anything else. They take seconds and already make DKA very likely.

steps.r: A **venous blood gas** shows the pH and bicarbonate, which confirm the acidosis part of the triad. HbA1c shows long-term control, not an acute crisis.

steps.lead: Chloe meets all three parts of the triad: glucose 28.4 (>11), ketones 5.2 (>3), pH 7.14 (<7.3) with bicarbonate 8 on her **venous gas**.

visual.title: Chloe's blood ketones
visual.label: Chloe 5.2
visual.caption: Above **3 mmol/L** is part of the diagnostic triad. Treatment continues until ketones are **below 0.6 mmol/L**.

steps.title: Bloods sent alongside the gas
steps.text: Raised urea and creatinine reflect dehydration. Raised WCC and CRP with positive nitrites point to a urinary infection as the precipitant.
**Anion gap** = Na − (Cl + HCO3) = 133 − (97 + 8) = **28** (normal about 8–14). Raised anion gap acidosis with normal lactate means the extra acid is ketones.

steps.q: Which additional test best identifies Chloe's precipitant?
steps.r: Dysuria, loin tenderness, fever and a positive dip suggest a urinary infection. Send an **MSU (and blood cultures)** before antibiotics so the precipitant can be treated.

steps.lead: Chloe's **potassium of 5.6** is the number everyone will watch. Her glucose, ketones, potassium and GCS are checked **every hour**, and treatment continues until she meets the resolution criteria.

steps.title: The hourly monitoring loop
nodes: Adjust potassium and glucose in fluids
steps.caption: Repeat every hour. A new drop in GCS or headache suggests cerebral oedema.

visual.title: Chloe's first 10 hours
visual.caption: Glucose falls fastest. Ketones below 0.6 and bicarbonate above 15 (with pH >7.3) are what define resolution.

steps.text: Her pH over the same hours: **7.14 → 7.19 → 7.27 → 7.34**. Only at hour 10 are all three resolution criteria met.

Glucose normalises **before** ketones and acidosis clear. At hour 6 Chloe's glucose is 12.8, but pH 7.27 and ketones 1.4 mean she has **not resolved**. Resolution is defined by pH, ketones and bicarbonate, not glucose.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (IV 0.9% sodium chloride, a bolus if hypotensive) and 'Which is the next most appropriate step?' (fixed-rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour, potassium replacement, adding 10% glucose when glucose <14, switching to SC insulin once resolved).

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
steps.r: **Fluids first**. She is hypotensive, so she gets a **500 mL 0.9% NaCl bolus stat**. Insulin comes after fluid resuscitation has started.

steps.lead: Chloe is hypotensive, so she gets the **500 mL bolus stat**. Once her BP improves to 104/66 she moves on to 1 L over 1 hour, then a further litre over 2 hours.

steps.title: DKA protocol in order
nodes: Potassium in fluids once level known
steps.caption: Fluids, insulin, potassium, glucose, switch, cause.

steps.q: Chloe weighs 60 kg. What rate should her fixed-rate insulin infusion run at?
steps.r: 0.1 units/kg/hour × 60 kg = **6 units/hour** of IV Actrapid.

steps.lead: Chloe starts **Actrapid at 6 units/hour**. Her **detemir is continued** at her usual times, and her **NovoRapid is stopped** while the infusion runs.

steps.text: Do not stop the long-acting basal insulin (detemir). Keeping it running avoids rebound ketosis when the infusion is stopped. It is the **short-acting** insulin that is paused.

steps.title: Repeat venous gas at 2 hours
steps.text: Her potassium has fallen from 5.6 to 4.1 in two hours of insulin.

steps.lead: Chloe's potassium is now 4.1 and falling, so she gets **40 mmol KCl in 1 L saline over 4 hours**. Glucose 12.8 (<14), so **10% glucose at 125 mL/hour** is added.

steps.q: Hour 6: glucose 12.8, ketones 1.4, pH 7.27. What happens to the insulin infusion?
o: Stop it and give SC NovoRapid
steps.r: She is still acidotic with ketones >0.6. The insulin is there to **clear ketones**, so it continues. The glucose infusion stops her going hypoglycaemic.

steps.lead: Hour 10: pH 7.34, ketones 0.4, bicarbonate 17 and she is eating. Switch to **SC insulin**, give **antibiotics for her pyelonephritis** and teach sick-day rules.
If Chloe were still ketotic or acidotic at **24 hours**, a senior endocrinologist would review her. If she developed a headache, falling GCS or bradycardia, the **fluids would be slowed**.
These four numbers run Chloe's whole admission: the triad to diagnose, pH/bicarbonate to grade, resolution criteria to stop, and 0.1 units/kg/hour to treat.

steps.text: Exam order of priority: **fluids → insulin → potassium → glucose when <14 → SC insulin once resolved and eating**. Bicarbonate is not part of the routine protocol.

science.exam: Expect applied 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' questions: the source of the acidosis (hepatic ketone production from fatty acids), Kussmaul breathing (respiratory compensation), high presenting potassium despite total body depletion, insulin-driven hypokalaemia, and cerebral oedema from osmotic shifts.

points: Next day on the ward Chloe asks:
'I only missed two days of insulin, why did I get so ill?'
You explain using her own results

steps.lead: Without insulin, Chloe's fat stores broke down unchecked. Her liver turned the fatty acids into ketones, which explains her **ketones of 5.2 and anion gap of 28**.

steps.title: From missed insulin to acidosis
nodes: Insulin deficiency (+ stress hormones from infection)
Free fatty acids to the liver
steps.caption: Acetone is volatile, which gives the fruity breath.

steps.lead: Chloe's polyuria, thirst, dry mouth, hypotension and raised urea all come from **osmotic diuresis**. She lost potassium in that urine as well.

steps.title: Hyperglycaemia to dehydration
nodes: No insulin: cells cannot take up glucose

steps.q: Chloe's total body potassium is low, yet her serum potassium was 5.6. Why?
o: Potassium shifts out of cells without insulin
steps.r: Without insulin (and with acidosis), potassium moves **out of cells** into the blood, so serum K looks normal or high while total body K is depleted.

steps.lead: This is why Chloe's potassium dropped from **5.6 to 4.1 in two hours**. The insulin switched on Na/K-ATPase and pushed potassium back into her cells.

visual.title: Chloe's serum potassium on insulin
visual.caption: A high-normal start, a steep fall once insulin runs, then stable because **40 mmol KCl per litre** was added from hour 2.

steps.text: Without replacement the fall would have continued into hypokalaemia, because her total body potassium was depleted by osmotic diuresis.

steps.lead: Chloe's respiratory rate of 30 and **pCO2 of 3.1 kPa** show her lungs blowing off CO2 to limit the fall in pH.

steps.text: In a metabolic acidosis a **low pCO2** shows the lungs are compensating. If the pCO2 is normal or high in a DKA stem, think about tiring or a second problem.

steps.lead: Chloe is an adult, so her risk is lower. A 9 year old having the same rapid fluid and insulin correction is at much greater risk of cerebral oedema.

steps.text: Cerebral oedema appears **during treatment**, often hours in. An improving child who develops headache, bradycardia or confusion has cerebral oedema until proven otherwise, even with normal glucose.

mcq.q: What is the most important precipitant of DKA?
mcq.r: Infection is the most important precipitant, followed by missed insulin doses and new diagnosis.

mcq.q: A pH of 7.15 and bicarbonate of 8 mmol/L in DKA is graded as:

o: Small T waves and prolonged PR interval
mcq.r: Hypokalaemia: small T waves, prolonged PR. Tall tented T waves and wide QRS are hyperkalaemia.

mcq.q: Which values make up the DKA diagnostic triad?
mcq.r: Glucose >11 mmol/L, blood ketones >3 mmol/L, pH <7.3.
The venous blood gas confirms the acidosis (pH and bicarbonate).
Resolution: pH >7.3, ketones <0.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate >15.0 mmol/L.

mcq.q: What is the first step in DKA management?
mcq.r: IV fluids (0.9% NaCl) are always the first step, as a 500 mL bolus if hypotensive.

mcq.q: When is 10% glucose added to the IV fluids?
mcq.r: When glucose <14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose (e.g. 125 mL/hour) while the insulin continues.

mcq.q: Why does serum potassium fall during DKA treatment?
o: Increased renal excretion from IV saline
Insulin drives potassium into cells via Na/K-ATPase
mcq.r: Insulin increases Na/K-ATPase activity, shifting potassium into cells, so replacement is needed.

prompts.q: What is DKA, who gets it, and what are the three main precipitants?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem rarely says 'DKA'; spot the young type 1 patient and look for the trigger.

points.p: Acute metabolic complication, most commonly of type 1 diabetes
points.why: It can occur in type 2 too, but the classic SBA patient is a young type 1 diabetic.

points.p: Infection is the most important precipitant
points.why: Look for fever, dysuria or cough in the stem and treat the source with antibiotics.

points.p: Missed insulin doses
points.why: Missed doses lead to education on sick-day rules once the episode resolves.

points.p: New diagnosis of type 1 diabetes
points.why: Weeks of thirst, polyuria and weight loss in a stem signal a first presentation.

prompts.q: What are the classic symptoms and signs of DKA?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: SBA stems hide DKA behind abdominal pain, vomiting and odd breathing; list the bedside clues.

points.p: Polyuria and polydipsia (thirst)
points.why: Osmotic diuresis from glucose in the urine causes both.

points.p: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain
points.why: Abdominal pain can mimic a surgical abdomen, a favourite distractor.

points.p: Kussmaul breathing (deep, rapid)
points.why: Deep sighing breaths with a clear chest point to metabolic acidosis, not a lung problem.

points.p: Fruity (acetone, pear drops) breath
points.why: Acetone from ketone breakdown gives the smell.

points.p: Dehydration with tachycardia and hypotension
points.why: Hypotension means a 500 ml bolus first, before anything else.

points.p: Confusion or drowsiness
points.why: Worsening confusion during treatment suggests cerebral oedema.

prompts.q: Which three results confirm DKA, with cut-offs, and how is severity graded?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: you need all three to diagnose; then grade on pH and bicarbonate (ketones above 3 in every grade).

points.p: Glucose above 11 mmol/L (or known diabetes)
points.why: Euglycaemic DKA exists (e.g. SGLT2 inhibitors), so a normal glucose does not fully exclude it.

points.p: Blood ketones above 3 mmol/L (or urine ketones 2+ or more)
points.why: Capillary blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate) are preferred over urine dipstick.

points.p: pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L
points.why: This is a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.

points.p: Mild: pH 7.2 to 7.29, bicarbonate below 15
points.why: Even mild DKA needs the full fluids plus insulin protocol.

points.p: Moderate: pH 7.1 to 7.19, bicarbonate below 10
points.why: Bicarbonate falls as the acid load rises.

points.p: Severe: pH below 7.1, bicarbonate below 5
points.why: Severe DKA warrants senior review and often HDU care.

prompts.q: How do you tell DKA from diabetic ketosis and from HHS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ask whether there is acidosis, and whether ketones or extreme glucose and osmolality dominate.

points.p: Diabetic ketosis: high glucose and ketones but no acidosis
points.why: Ketosis is managed with SC insulin, fluids and monitoring, not the full DKA protocol.

points.p: HHS: very high glucose and osmolality, little or no ketosis or acidosis
points.why: HHS is typically an older type 2 patient, developing over days with severe dehydration.

points.p: DKA: acidosis (pH below 7.3) with ketones above 3
points.why: The acidosis is what makes it DKA rather than ketosis.

prompts.q: What are the key complications of DKA and its treatment?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: potassium kills; know the ECG picture of both extremes and spot cerebral oedema.

points.p: Hypokalaemia, the most common: small T waves, prolonged PR
points.why: Caused mainly by insulin driving potassium into cells during treatment.

points.p: Hyperkalaemia: tall tented T waves, widened QRS
points.why: Seen at presentation from acidosis and insulin lack.

points.p: Cerebral oedema: headache, seizures, falling GCS, bradycardia
points.why: Rare but life-threatening, more common in children.

prompts.q: What are the first-line bedside tests and the confirmatory test?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bedside capillary tests first, then a venous gas confirms; an arterial stab is not needed.

points.p: Capillary blood glucose (BM)
points.why: Hourly glucose monitoring continues throughout treatment.

points.p: Capillary blood ketones
points.why: Blood ketones are more accurate than urine ketones and guide treatment response.

points.p: Venous blood gas confirms the acidosis
points.why: VBG pH and bicarbonate are accurate enough; ABG only if oxygenation is a concern.

points.p: Bloods: U&Es (potassium), CRP; look for the precipitant
points.why: Potassium guides replacement; CRP and cultures hunt for infection.

prompts.q: What do you monitor during treatment, and what defines resolution?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: resolution needs all three numbers; any change in mental state means think cerebral oedema.

points.p: Hourly glucose, ketones, electrolytes (especially potassium) and mental status
points.why: Ketones should fall by about 0.5 mmol/L per hour on correct treatment.

points.p: Resolution: pH above 7.3
points.why: pH and bicarbonate recover after ketones clear.

points.p: Resolution: ketones below 0.6 mmol/L
points.why: 0.6 is the normal upper limit, so ketones must be normal.

points.p: Resolution: bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L
points.why: Only once all three are met do you switch to subcutaneous insulin.

prompts.q: What is the first fluid step for a hypotensive patient, and for a stable one?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fluids always come first, before insulin; hypotension changes the volume and speed.

points.p: IV 0.9% sodium chloride is the critical first step
points.why: Fluids before insulin: insulin into a dry patient worsens shock as glucose and water move into cells.

points.p: Hypotensive/unstable: 500 ml bolus stat (or 10 ml/kg over 15 min)
points.why: Reassess after each bolus and repeat if still hypotensive.

points.p: Stable: 1 L over 1 hour, then a further litre over 2 hours
points.why: The infusion slows progressively over the following hours.

prompts.q: What insulin is given, at what rate, and what happens to the usual insulins?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fixed-rate, weight-based; keep the long-acting going.

points.p: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (Actrapid)
points.why: Fixed, not variable (sliding scale): the target is clearing ketones, not just glucose.

points.p: 0.1 units/kg/hour
points.why: For a 70 kg patient that is 7 units/hour.

points.p: Continue long-acting insulin (e.g. detemir)
points.why: Continuing basal insulin prevents rebound ketosis when the infusion stops.

points.p: Stop short-acting insulin (e.g. NovoRapid)
points.why: The IV infusion replaces the short-acting insulin.

prompts.q: When do you add potassium and 10% glucose, and what next once resolved?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: insulin keeps going; you feed it glucose and potassium rather than stopping it.

points.p: Potassium chloride added to saline once the level is known (e.g. 40 mmol in 1 L over 4 hours)
points.why: Insulin lowers serum potassium; standard ward maximum is usually 10 mmol/hour.

points.p: Add 10% glucose when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L
points.why: Run it alongside saline (e.g. 125 ml/hour) so insulin can continue clearing ketones without hypoglycaemia.

points.p: Once resolved and eating, switch to subcutaneous insulin
points.why: Overlap the SC dose with the infusion so there is never a gap.

points.p: Treat the precipitant: antibiotics for infection, education on missed doses
points.why: Not resolving within 24 hours means senior endocrinology review.

points.p: Cerebral oedema: slow the IV fluids
points.why: Rapid osmotic shifts are blamed, so fluid rate is reduced.

prompts.q: Why does insulin deficiency cause ketoacidosis and dehydration?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one cause (no insulin) explains the glucose, the ketones and the fluid loss.

points.p: Insulin deficiency stops glucose entering cells, causing hyperglycaemia
points.why: Counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol) push glucose up further.

points.p: Unrestrained lipolysis releases free fatty acids, converted to ketones in the liver
points.why: Ketones are acids, so they lower pH.

points.p: Ketones cause a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis
points.why: The gap is raised by unmeasured ketone anions.

points.p: Glycosuria causes osmotic diuresis, so dehydration and electrolyte loss
points.why: This drives polyuria, thirst and hypotension.

points.p: Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation, blowing off CO2
points.why: Low pCO2 on the gas shows the compensation.

prompts.q: Why is potassium high at presentation but falls with insulin?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: serum potassium lies; the whole body is depleted.

points.p: Insulin lack and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, so serum K is normal or high
points.why: Without insulin, Na/K-ATPase activity falls and potassium leaks out.

points.p: Total body potassium is depleted (lost in urine and vomit)
points.why: A normal serum level hides a large deficit.

points.p: Insulin drives potassium into cells (Na/K-ATPase), so it falls rapidly
points.why: This is why potassium is replaced and checked hourly.

glossary.DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: high glucose, high ketones and metabolic acidosis caused by severe insulin deficiency.
glossary.HHS: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: very high glucose and osmolality with severe dehydration but little ketosis, usually in type 2 diabetes.
glossary.Diabetic ketosis: Raised glucose and ketones without acidosis; treated with subcutaneous insulin and fluids rather than the DKA protocol.
glossary.Euglycaemic DKA: DKA with near-normal glucose, classically caused by SGLT2 inhibitor drugs.
glossary.SGLT2: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2; inhibitor drugs (e.g. dapagliflozin) lower glucose via the urine but can trigger euglycaemic DKA.
glossary.Kussmaul breathing: Deep, laboured breathing that blows off CO2 to compensate for metabolic acidosis.
glossary.Anion gap: (Na + K) minus (Cl + HCO3); a raised gap means extra unmeasured acid such as ketones.
glossary.Metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH caused by excess acid or lost bicarbonate, rather than by retained CO2.
glossary.Ketones: Acidic fuel molecules made by the liver from fatty acids when cells cannot use glucose.
glossary.Ketonaemia: Ketones in the blood; above 3 mmol/L is one of the DKA diagnostic criteria.
glossary.Beta-hydroxybutyrate: The main ketone body in DKA, measured by capillary blood ketone meters.
glossary.Lipolysis: Breakdown of stored fat into free fatty acids and glycerol, switched on when insulin is absent.
glossary.Osmotic diuresis: Excess urine output because glucose in the urine pulls water with it, causing dehydration.
glossary.Glycosuria: Glucose in the urine, which occurs once blood glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorption threshold.
glossary.Pear drops: Sweet, fruity breath smell caused by exhaled acetone in ketoacidosis.
glossary.Osmolality: Concentration of dissolved particles in blood; very high in HHS, and rapid changes can cause cerebral oedema.
glossary.VBG: Venous blood gas: a gas taken from a vein, accurate enough for pH, bicarbonate and potassium in DKA.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: blood from an artery, needed when oxygenation must be assessed.
glossary.Capillary: Finger-prick sample used at the bedside for glucose and ketone measurements.
glossary.BM: Bedside capillary blood glucose reading from a finger-prick test.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood test for sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine to assess kidney function.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: a blood marker of inflammation, raised in infection.
glossary.Bicarbonate: The main blood buffer (HCO3); it is used up by ketoacids, so a low level shows acidosis severity.
glossary.pCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in blood; low in DKA because Kussmaul breathing blows CO2 off.
glossary.Lactate: Product of anaerobic metabolism; a raised level suggests poor perfusion or sepsis rather than ketoacidosis.
glossary.FRIII: Fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion: weight-based IV insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) used to clear ketones in DKA.
glossary.Actrapid: Soluble short-acting human insulin, used in the IV infusion for DKA.
glossary.Detemir: Long-acting basal insulin (Levemir), continued during DKA treatment to prevent rebound ketosis.
glossary.NovoRapid: Rapid-acting mealtime insulin (aspart), stopped while the IV insulin infusion runs.
glossary.Basal insulin: Long-acting background insulin that covers needs between meals and overnight.
glossary.Sliding scale: Variable-rate insulin adjusted to glucose; not used in DKA, where a fixed rate is needed.
glossary.0.9% sodium chloride: Normal saline: the standard IV fluid used first to rehydrate in DKA.
glossary.Bolus: A set volume of fluid given quickly, e.g. 500 ml stat in a hypotensive patient.
glossary.Stat: Immediately, given as a single dose now.
glossary.Potassium chloride: Potassium salt added to IV fluids to replace potassium lost and driven into cells during treatment.
glossary.Na/K-ATPase: Cell membrane pump that moves potassium into cells; insulin increases its activity.
glossary.Hypokalaemia: Low blood potassium; the commonest DKA complication, causing small T waves, prolonged PR and arrhythmias.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: High blood potassium; causes tall tented T waves and widened QRS, risking cardiac arrest.
glossary.Tented T waves: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves on ECG, an early sign of hyperkalaemia.
glossary.PR interval: ECG time from start of atrial to start of ventricular activation; prolonged in hypokalaemia.
glossary.QRS: ECG complex showing ventricular depolarisation; widens in severe hyperkalaemia.
glossary.Cerebral oedema: Brain swelling, a rare but deadly DKA complication in children, linked to rapid osmotic shifts during treatment.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, scored 3 to 15, measuring eye, verbal and motor responses to grade consciousness.
glossary.Bradycardia: Heart rate below 60 bpm; in DKA it may signal raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema.
glossary.Hypotension: Low blood pressure; in DKA it means severe dehydration and calls for a fluid bolus.
glossary.Tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 bpm, here a sign of dehydration.
glossary.Precipitant: The trigger that tipped the patient into DKA, such as infection or missed insulin.
glossary.Sick-day rules: Advice for diabetics when unwell: never stop insulin, check ketones and glucose often, and seek help early.
glossary.HDU: High dependency unit: a ward between general ward and intensive care, used for severe DKA.

technique.stem: A 16 year old boy has a 2 day history of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing thirst. He has been passing urine frequently and has lost 4 kg over the past month. He has no past medical history. He is drowsy and his breathing is deep and rapid. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis. The labs are a glucose, ketones and a gas, which tells you this is a metabolic emergency question.

clues: lost 4 kg over the past month
steps.x: Thirst, polyuria and weight loss in a teenager suggest a **new presentation of type 1 diabetes**. Drowsiness and deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul respiration) suggest acidosis. In the labs, ketones 4.8 (>3) and pH 7.18 (<7.3) complete the triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose >11 + ketones >3 + pH <7.3 = **DKA** (moderate: pH 7.1–7.19, bicarbonate <10).

elim: Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and vomiting but not a glucose of 31 with ketoacidosis. DKA abdominal pain is a classic mimic.
Diabetic ketosis has raised glucose and ketones but **no acidosis**. His pH is 7.18.
HHS occurs in older type 2 patients over days to weeks, without significant ketonaemia or acidosis.
Salicylate poisoning can cause a metabolic acidosis and hyperventilation, but there is no ingestion history and it does not explain glucose 31 with weight loss.

steps.x: **B: Diabetic ketoacidosis.** Rule: all three of glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3. If pH is normal it is ketosis, not DKA.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 18 hours. She has type 1 diabetes and has had a cough with green sputum for 4 days. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 108/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her capillary glucose is 24.1 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 4.1 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for the test that **confirms** the diagnosis, not the first bedside test. The bedside tests have already been done in the stem.
Type 1 diabetes with a chest infection (precipitant), tachypnoea, glucose >11 and ketones >3. Two parts of the triad are present. The missing piece is **acidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: You need a pH and bicarbonate, so a **venous blood gas**.

elim: An abdominal X-ray does not help with DKA abdominal pain and gives no acid–base information.
HbA1c reflects glycaemic control over about 3 months, not an acute crisis.
Serum osmolality is key in HHS, but it does not show the acidosis needed to diagnose DKA.
A urine dipstick shows ketones and glucose but cannot measure pH or bicarbonate, so it cannot confirm acidosis.

steps.x: **E: Venous blood gas.** Rule: bedside capillary glucose and ketones first, then a VBG to confirm the acidosis.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man is brought to the emergency department with vomiting and confusion. He has type 1 diabetes and ran out of insulin 3 days ago. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He weighs 70 kg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: 'Initial management' means the very first thing you do. In DKA that is a protocol with a fixed order.

clues: ran out of insulin 3 days ago
steps.x: In the labs, pH 7.09 and bicarbonate 4 = severe DKA (pH <7.1, bicarbonate <5) in a man who is **hypotensive and tachycardic**, so he is haemodynamically unstable. Potassium is already high-normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluids first. Because he is hypotensive, he needs a **500 mL 0.9% NaCl bolus stat**.

elim: The fixed-rate insulin infusion is the **second** step, started after fluid resuscitation is under way.
10% glucose is added only when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. His glucose is 33.
Potassium is given once levels are known and is not needed when K is already 5.4. It is never the first step.
Bicarbonate is not part of the routine DKA protocol. Fluids and insulin correct the acidosis.

steps.x: **B: 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL bolus.** Rule: fluids, then insulin, then potassium, then glucose when <14.

technique.stem: A 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis after a week of gastroenteritis. Her pulse rate is 120 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. She is started on intravenous fluids and a fixed-rate insulin infusion.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her raised serum potassium at presentation?
o: Extracellular shift due to insulin deficiency

steps.x: It asks for a **mechanism** that explains a lab value in the vignette, so this is an applied science question.
DKA with vomiting and diarrhoea means potassium has been **lost**. She is dehydrated (tachycardic, BP 96/60). Yet serum K in the labs is 5.9. Creatinine is normal, so renal failure is not the cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lack of insulin (and acidosis) moves potassium **out of cells** into the blood. Total body K is depleted, but serum K is normal or high.

elim: Adrenal insufficiency can raise potassium, but nothing in the stem suggests it, and DKA explains the result fully.
Diet does not cause hyperkalaemia in a person with normal kidneys, and she has been vomiting.
Haemolysis is a lab artefact. It is a distractor when there is a clear physiological cause.
Total body potassium is **depleted** in DKA because of osmotic diuresis and vomiting. This is the classic trap.

steps.x: **C: Extracellular shift due to insulin deficiency.** Rule: in DKA serum K can be high, but the body's stores are empty. Insulin will drop it fast, so replace it.

practice.stem: A 20 year old man with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for 24 hours. He is drowsy, with deep rapid breathing. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 90/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <5 with ketones >3 = **severe** DKA. Moderate DKA would be pH 7.1–7.19 with bicarbonate <10. Diabetic ketosis has no acidosis.

steps.x: Diagnosis question, but four DKA options: this is really about **severity grading**.
Type 1 + Kussmaul breathing + shock = DKA. Now grade it on **pH and bicarbonate**: pH 7.04, bicarbonate 4.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ketones >3 and pH <7.3 = DKA. pH <7.1 and bicarbonate <5 = **severe**.

elim: Ketosis has **no acidosis**. pH here is 7.04.
HHS: older type 2, huge glucose, no significant ketones or acidosis.
Mild is pH 7.2–7.29, bicarbonate <15.
Moderate is pH 7.1–7.19, bicarbonate <10.

steps.x: **E: Severe DKA.** Severity = pH <7.1, bicarbonate <5 (mild <15, moderate <10, severe <5).

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has had a sore throat and runny nose for 2 days. Her home glucose readings have been high and she has vomited once today. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3 is DKA; pH 7.2–7.29 with bicarbonate <15 is **mild**. Diabetic ketosis would have a normal pH.

steps.x: Diagnosis, with ketosis and three grades of DKA as options. Check the **pH first**.
Infection is the commonest DKA precipitant. She looks well, but the **gas decides**: pH 7.26, bicarbonate 13.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose 17 (>11), ketones 3.4 (>3), pH 7.26 (<7.3) = DKA. pH 7.2–7.29, bicarbonate <15 = **mild**.

elim: Ketosis means **no acidosis**. Her pH is 7.26, so she is acidotic.
HHS: older type 2, glucose often >30, no ketoacidosis.
Moderate needs pH 7.1–7.19 and bicarbonate <10.
Starvation ketosis has a **normal glucose** and mild ketones.

steps.x: **C: Mild DKA.** Looking well does not exclude DKA. Always check the pH: acidosis turns ketosis into DKA.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting for 24 hours. He stopped his insulin because he was not eating. He is drowsy and his breath smells of acetone. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 94/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his breathing?
practice.e: DKA causes a metabolic acidosis; the lungs compensate by blowing off CO2 with **Kussmaul breathing** (deep, sighing, rapid). Shallow, slow breathing is the opposite.

steps.x: Asks for an **examination finding**, so first name the condition, then its classic sign.
Missed insulin + acetone breath + glucose 30, ketones 5.6, pH 7.12 = **moderate DKA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Metabolic acidosis → respiratory compensation → **Kussmaul breathing**: deep, sighing respirations.

elim: Wheeze is airway narrowing (asthma, COPD), not acidosis.
Slow, shallow breathing would retain CO2 and worsen the acidosis.
Stridor is upper airway obstruction.
Unilateral reduced air entry suggests effusion, collapse or pneumothorax.

steps.x: **B: Deep, sighing respirations.** Kussmaul breathing = blowing off CO2 to raise the pH.

practice.stem: A 17 year old girl with type 1 diabetes has a 24 hour history of severe central abdominal pain and vomiting. Her abdomen is diffusely tender but soft, with no guarding. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 100/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Abdominal pain and vomiting are classic DKA features. Glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3 confirm **DKA**. The soft abdomen and normal amylase argue against a surgical cause.

steps.x: Diagnosis. Abdominal pain in a type 1 diabetic: **check the ketones before the surgeons**.

clues: severe central abdominal pain and vomiting
steps.x: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, fast breathing. The labs show glucose 24.6, ketones 4.4, pH 7.22.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: DKA triad met (mild: pH 7.2–7.29, bicarbonate <15). The pain is **part of DKA**.

elim: Gastroenteritis does not cause ketones 4.4 with pH 7.22.
HHS has no significant ketones or acidosis and occurs in older type 2 patients.
Perforation gives a rigid abdomen with guarding.
Obstruction gives distension and colicky pain, not a ketoacidosis.

steps.x: **A: DKA.** Type 1 + abdominal pain + vomiting + fast breathing: think DKA and check ketones and a gas.

practice.stem: A 23 year old man with type 1 diabetes has a 4 day history of fever and a cough productive of rusty sputum, followed by vomiting and abdominal pain. He has taken his insulin every day. He has deep, rapid breathing and bronchial breathing at the right base. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his diabetic ketoacidosis?
practice.e: **Infection** is the most important precipitant of DKA. Rusty sputum, bronchial breathing and right lower zone consolidation mean **pneumonia**. He took his insulin, so omission is unlikely, and the vomiting began after the chest symptoms, pointing away from gastroenteritis.

steps.x: Asks for the **precipitant**, not the diagnosis. DKA is already given.

clues: He has taken his insulin every day
bronchial breathing at the right base
steps.x: Rusty sputum, bronchial breathing and right lower zone consolidation = **pneumonia**. Insulin was taken.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection is the most important DKA precipitant. Here it is a **chest infection**.

elim: Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain radiating to the back, not a consolidation.
Vomiting started **after** the chest symptoms.
He took his insulin every day.
No urinary symptoms; the source is the chest.

steps.x: **D: Lower respiratory tract infection.** In every DKA, look for the precipitant: infection first, then missed insulin, then new diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 9 year old girl is being treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with intravenous fluids and a fixed-rate insulin infusion. Six hours into treatment she complains of a severe headache and becomes confused. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 52 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Headache, confusion and **bradycardia** during DKA treatment in a child is cerebral oedema, caused by rapid osmotic shifts. Glucose and potassium are normal, which rules out hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. She is afebrile, which makes meningitis unlikely.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a **new problem during DKA treatment**. Think treatment complications.
A child, hours into treatment, with headache, confusion and **bradycardia**: a neurological complication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rapid osmotic shifts during correction → **cerebral oedema**, commoner in children.

elim: Glucose is 10.6, not low.
Potassium is 4.0, normal.
Afebrile and timing fits treatment, not infection.
No thunderclap onset; the timing links it to treatment.

steps.x: **A: Cerebral oedema.** Child + DKA treatment + headache, confusion, bradycardia = cerebral oedema. Slow the fluids.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man with type 1 diabetes arrives at the emergency department with 12 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has missed his insulin since yesterday. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: First-line tests in suspected DKA are bedside **capillary ketones** and capillary glucose, which give results in seconds. A VBG then confirms the diagnosis. HbA1c and imaging do not help in the acute setting.

steps.x: Asks for the **initial** test: the fastest one that changes management.
Type 1 + vomiting + missed insulin + fast breathing = suspected DKA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line in suspected DKA: bedside **capillary ketones** (with capillary glucose). Then a VBG.

elim: Abdominal X-ray does not diagnose DKA.
HbA1c shows long-term control, not the acute state.
Amylase looks for pancreatitis, not the first test here.
Urine culture finds a precipitant later, not first.

steps.x: **B: Capillary blood ketones.** Bedside ketones and glucose first, VBG to confirm.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain and deep sighing respirations. She has missed her insulin for 2 days. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Her capillary glucose is 26.3 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 5.0 mmol/L. Her serum lactate is 1.4 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on venous blood gas?
practice.e: Ketone bodies are unmeasured acids, so DKA causes a **raised anion gap** metabolic acidosis: 134 − (98 + 7) = 29. A normal anion gap acidosis suggests bicarbonate loss (e.g. diarrhoea). Kussmaul breathing lowers pCO2 as compensation, but the primary problem is metabolic.

steps.x: Asks for the **gas pattern**. Work out the anion gap.
Ketones 5.0 + low bicarbonate = metabolic acidosis. Lactate is normal, so the acid is ketones.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anion gap = 134 − (98 + 7) = **29** (raised). So **raised anion gap metabolic acidosis**.

elim: Bicarbonate is 7, low: acidosis, not alkalosis.
Normal anion gap acidosis is bicarbonate loss (e.g. diarrhoea). Gap here is 29.
Respiratory acidosis needs CO2 retention; she is blowing CO2 off.
Low pCO2 is compensation, not the primary problem.

steps.x: **C: Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.** Ketones are unmeasured acids, so DKA raises the anion gap.

practice.stem: A 28 year old man with type 1 diabetes is diagnosed with moderate diabetic ketoacidosis. He weighs 80 kg. He has received 1 litre of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and his BP is now 118/72 mmHg. He usually takes insulin detemir twice daily and insulin aspart with meals.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Variable-rate IV insulin titrated to glucose
practice.e: After fluids, start a **fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour** (8 units/hour for 80 kg). Detemir is continued; aspart is stopped. A variable-rate infusion is titrated to glucose and is not the DKA regimen, because the aim is to clear ketones.

steps.x: Asks for the **next step**. Fluids are already running.

clues: received 1 litre of intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride
steps.x: Moderate DKA, fluids started, BP recovered. Next comes **insulin**, dosed by weight.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fixed-rate IV insulin **0.1 units/kg/hour** = 8 units/hour. Keep detemir, stop aspart.

elim: 1 unit/kg/hour is ten times the dose.
Long-acting detemir is **continued**.
SC rapid-acting insulin is stopped during DKA treatment.
Variable-rate is titrated to glucose; DKA needs fixed-rate to clear ketones.

steps.x: **A: Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour.** Fluids first, then fixed-rate insulin, then potassium.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman is 5 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium and a fixed-rate insulin infusion. She feels better and her vomiting has stopped. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. She has received 3 litres of intravenous fluid so far.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue insulin infusion and add 10% glucose
Start subcutaneous insulin and stop infusion
practice.e: Glucose has fallen below **14 mmol/L**, but she is still acidotic with ketones >0.6. Add **10% glucose** (e.g. 125 mL/hour) alongside the saline and **continue the insulin** to clear ketones. She does not meet the criteria to switch to SC insulin yet.

steps.x: Asks for the **next step** mid-treatment. Compare each result with its target.

clues: She feels better and her vomiting has stopped
steps.x: Glucose 12.5 (<14) but ketones 2.4, pH 7.22: **still in DKA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Glucose <14 → add **10% glucose** (125 mL/hour) and **keep the insulin going** to clear ketones.

elim: 50% glucose is for hypoglycaemia; she is not hypoglycaemic.
Not resolved (pH <7.3, ketones >0.6), so no SC switch yet.
Stopping insulin lets ketones rise again.
Saline is still needed; 10% glucose is added alongside.

steps.x: **B: Continue insulin, add 10% glucose.** Glucose guides the dextrose; ketones guide the insulin.

practice.stem: A 21 year old woman is 11 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by a urinary tract infection. She is alert and asking for breakfast. She is receiving oral antibiotics. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. She usually takes insulin glargine once daily and insulin aspart with meals.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue fixed-rate insulin for a further 24 hours
practice.e: pH >7.3, ketones <0.6 and bicarbonate >15 mean DKA has **resolved**. She is eating, so switch to **subcutaneous insulin**. Senior endocrinology review is for DKA not resolved within 24 hours.

steps.x: Asks for the **next step** late in treatment. Check the resolution criteria.

clues: She is alert and asking for breakfast
steps.x: pH 7.35 (>7.3), ketones 0.3 (<0.6), bicarbonate 18 (>15): **resolved**. And she is eating.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: DKA resolved + eating = **switch to subcutaneous insulin**.

elim: No need: DKA has resolved.
Glucose 9.8 is fine; DKA is over.
Senior review is for DKA **not resolved by 24 hours**.
Bicarbonate is not part of DKA treatment.

steps.x: **E: Switch to SC insulin.** Resolution = pH >7.3, ketones <0.6, bicarbonate >15.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has been unable to afford her insulin for 4 days. She has vomiting and abdominal pain, and her breath smells of pear drops. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her acidosis?
o: Hepatic ketone body production from fatty acids
practice.e: Insulin deficiency allows unrestrained **lipolysis**. The free fatty acids are converted to **ketone bodies in the liver**, causing a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis. Lactate is normal, pCO2 is low (not retained) and creatinine is normal.

steps.x: Asks for the **mechanism of the acidosis**. Use the gas and lactate.

clues: unable to afford her insulin for 4 days
steps.x: No insulin, pear-drop breath, ketones 5.8, lactate normal, pCO2 low: **ketoacidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No insulin → unrestrained lipolysis → fatty acids → **ketone bodies in the liver**.

elim: pCO2 is 3.0, low: she is blowing CO2 off.
No diarrhoea; bicarbonate loss gives a normal anion gap.
Lactate 1.5 is normal.
Creatinine 98 is normal.

steps.x: **C: Hepatic ketone production from fatty acids.** Insulin deficiency → lipolysis → ketones → raised anion gap acidosis.
